claims.claim: Humour depends on surprise, and a predictive model that regurgitates tropes cannot supply it.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: AI is only adept at regurgitating tropes

claims.claim: Comedy runs on unspoken subtext that a text-only model neither carries nor reads.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)

claims.feature: placeless voice; no audience or location
claims.claim: LLM material has no sense of where or to whom it is spoken.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: everywhere and nowhere all at once

claims.feature: moderation flattens dark and minority-coded material
claims.claim: Safety filters refused dark material and stripped out gay-coded language, which comedians read as censorship of their own identities.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: taking out the gay language of it

claims.feature: cultural defaults survive a language switch
claims.claim: Switching the conversation into Indian languages left the character names un-localised.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: it didn’t automatically change the names

claims.feature: no pride or uniqueness in AI-assisted material
claims.claim: Most participants felt neither pride nor uniqueness in material co-written with the model; the Creativity Support Index was mediocre.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: did not feel pride in the material written with AI

claims.feature: delivery and surprise absent from a text-only medium
claims.claim: The paper names delivery and surprise as critical comedic elements a text-only model cannot provide.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)

claims.claim: Models reproduce what is on the surface of a literary story while the subtext is absent or wrongly interpreted.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.feature: unreliable narrator taken at face value
claims.claim: All three models score lower on stories with unreliable narrators and repeat the narrator's self-description as fact.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: the narrator is not really to be trusted

claims.feature: vague stock phrases instead of specifics
claims.claim: Weak summaries substitute stock phrases for the specific content of the story (64 'vague' span errors across models).
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: stock phrases or stand-ins rather than accurate, specific summary

claims.feature: schoolroom over-analysis that misses the feeling
claims.claim: Summaries pile on interpretive claims in a classroom register while missing the story's larger emotional point.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: like a high school english class

claims.claim: Claude imposed a heteronormative monogamous reading of an interaction over what the text actually says.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.claim: An implied death was rendered as a deliberate choice to stay at the summit.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.feature: errors cluster in what characters did and felt
claims.claim: Most faithfulness errors fall in Action and Feeling, the categories requiring interpretation of characters' deeds and reactions.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: most faithfulness errors across the models are in Action and Feeling

claims.feature: unsupported analysis even in top-rated summaries
claims.claim: Summaries rated 4/4 for analysis still contained on average at least one analysis error (104 unsupported-analysis spans in total).
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: at least one error in analysis on average
